title: Bolivia’s Post-MAS Transition Is at Risk
gist: Nine months into Rodrigo Paz Pereira's presidency, Bolivia's post-MAS transition is unraveling into a combined crisis of governance, economic credibility and public safety: fuel shortages have returned, Congress is paralyzed, organized crime is escalating, and the personalism and institutional weakness of the MAS era have endured despite the party's electoral defeat.

insights.claim: Rodrigo Paz Pereira ended the two-decade dominance of Bolivia's Movement Toward Socialism (MAS) party and initially survived a severe inherited economic crisis, but nine months in that early optimism now requires substantial revision.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: A narrative flip from 'fragile opening' to 'combined crisis' is the core repricing signal for Bolivian sovereign and macro risk.
insights.quote: That assessment now requires substantial revision.
insights.locator: That assessment now requires substantial revision

insights.claim: Bolivia is not stabilizing but entering a combined crisis of governance, economic credibility and public safety.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: A simultaneous three-front breakdown compounds risk faster than any single crisis, arguing for a wider risk premium on Bolivian exposure.
insights.quote: Bolivia is not stabilizing. It is entering a combined crisis of governance, economic credibility, and public safety.

insights.claim: The personalism, corruption and institutional weakness that characterized the MAS years have endured past the party's electoral defeat and are now seriously undermining Bolivian state capacity.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Removing a party without removing entrenched practices means the reform thesis was mispriced; institutional decay is the durable driver of instability.
insights.quote: removing the MAS did not remove the political practices that the MAS ingrained in the state
insights.locator: Paz’s victory showed that Bolivians wanted change

insights.claim: Paz's Christian Democratic Party won Bolivia's presidency but not the legislative strength to govern alone, and nearly a year later the country still lacks the agreements needed to confront structural problems, turning Congress into an arena of paralysis.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Without a legislative coalition, no credible reform or budget can pass, capping any recovery scenario for Bolivian assets.
insights.quote: Congress has become an arena of paralysis rather than reform
insights.locator: The government has failed to turn its election victory

insights.claim: Vice President Edmand Lara increasingly acts as a political adversary and is positioning himself as a populist opponent to President Paz rather than a governing partner.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: An internal VP rival raises the odds of a fractured or shortened administration, a key tail risk for continuity of reforms.
insights.quote: His own vice president, Edmand Lara, increasingly acts as a political adversary rather than a governing partner.
insights.locator: His own vice president, Edmand Lara

insights.claim: Social movements recently subjected Bolivia to 53 days of blockades demanding Paz's resignation, demonstrating their retained capacity to paralyze the country.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: 53-day blockade capacity is a recurring supply-chain and political-stability shock that can force policy reversals at any time.
insights.quote: Social movements recently subjected the country to 53 days of blockades demanding Paz’s resignation.
insights.locator: Social movements recently subjected the country

insights.claim: Paz eliminated Bolivia's long-standing fuel subsidies, a major step, but low domestic investment and production have deepened import dependence, caused foreign currency reserves to dwindle, and brought long lines at gas stations back.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Dwindling FX reserves plus renewed fuel shortages point to balance-of-payments and currency stress, the sharpest near-term macro risk.
insights.quote: This is deepening the country’s dependence on imports and causing foreign currency reserves to dwindle.
insights.locator: Bolivia’s energy crisis is a good example

insights.claim: The return of long gas-station lines is a visible signal that the dramatic first-months measures of Paz's government left Bolivia's underlying energy problems unresolved.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Fuel queues are a real-time, observable indicator that headline reforms have not fixed the production and reserves problem.
insights.quote: Long lines at gas stations have returned
insights.locator: Long lines at gas stations have returned

insights.claim: Bolivia occupies a strategic position in the South American cocaine economy, connecting production zones with Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and ultimately European markets.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Bolivia's role as a transit hub means its security breakdown has cross-border spillover into regional trafficking and stability.
insights.quote: Bolivia occupies a strategic position in the South American cocaine economy, connecting production zones with Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and ultimately European markets.

insights.claim: The Brazilian criminal groups Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho appear to have expanded their reach in Bolivia, and the proliferation of contract killings and sicariato-style violence signals a disturbing new normal.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Foreign cartel expansion plus rising sicariato is an early marker of state-capacity erosion that precedes broader security collapse.
insights.quote: The Brazilian criminal groups Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho, for example, seem to have expanded their reach in Bolivia.

insights.claim: Increasingly brazen killings raise the possibility that Bolivia could begin experiencing a security breakdown like that of Ecuador or Colombia.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: An Ecuador-style security implosion is the explicit downside scenario to watch for regional contagion and risk pricing.
insights.quote: Bolivia could begin experiencing a security breakdown like that of Ecuador or Colombia
insights.locator: Increasingly brazen killings raise the possibility

insights.claim: A scandal over Argentine political consultant Fernando Cerimedo, alleged to have orchestrated a sicario-style hit on his pregnant girlfriend and legal adviser in Santa Cruz, has reinforced public perception that powerful consultants manipulate informal government channels for their own ends.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: The scandal is a case study in Bolivia's 'crippled institutionality' and the corrosive role of campaign operatives in weak states.
insights.quote: powerful consultants and special interests are manipulating informal channels in government for their own ends

insights.claim: Cerimedo moved within right-wing networks that included figures connected to Donald Trump's political operation and other conservative movements in Latin America, tying the scandal to internationalized ideological campaign networks.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: Links to Trump-aligned networks make this a signal of how transnational consultant politics is spreading into Andean governance.
insights.quote: Cerimedo moved within right-wing networks that included figures connected to Donald Trump’s political operation and other conservative movements in Latin America.
insights.locator: The public’s reaction to the Cerimedo allegations

insights.claim: Political consultants can win elections but cannot substitute for political parties, professional bureaucracies or functioning institutions, and when they try they deliver only Pyrrhic victories.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: The 'Pyrrhic victory' framing warns that electoral wins without institution-building are not durable political outcomes.
insights.quote: Political consultants can help win elections, but they cannot substitute for political parties, professional bureaucracies or functioning institutions.
insights.locator: This should provoke reflection in Washington

insights.claim: Paz reversed Bolivia's anti-US trajectory by restoring close relations with Washington and international financial institutions and renewing counternarcotics cooperation, after Evo Morales expelled the U.S. ambassador and the DEA in 2008.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: A restored US relationship and IFI access is the positive catalyst for financing, but the author warns it may have little impact without institutional reform.
insights.quote: Morales had expelled the U.S. ambassador and the Drug Enforcement Administration in 2008, and Paz reversed that trajectory
insights.locator: The U.S. understandably welcomed Paz’s election

insights.claim: The author warns that if Paz fails to right the ship of state, the next administration could be even more damaging than the MAS governments, with VP Lara as a populist opponent, Morales still destabilizing, a fragmented opposition, and strengthening criminal networks.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: The base-case downside is a successor worse than the MAS era, defining the tail risk for anyone with Bolivian exposure over the coming decade.
insights.quote: the next administration could be even more damaging than the MAS governments that came before
insights.locator: The danger now is that if Paz fails

insights.claim: Gamarra prescribes that Paz must build a governing coalition, pass credible legislation, institutionalize anti-corruption mechanisms and lay out a national security strategy commensurate with the organized-crime threat to avoid a descent into instability.
insights.speaker: Eduardo A. Gamarra
insights.so_what: These four benchmarks are the concrete checklist to monitor for whether Bolivia's trajectory improves or deteriorates.
insights.quote: He will need to stand up a governing coalition, pass credible legislation, institutionalize anti-corruption mechanisms, and lay out a national security strategy
insights.locator: Paz still has time to reverse course
